summary: This informational document surveys short- and middle-range radio technologies suitable for Reliable and Available Wireless service in DetNet. It describes their characteristics and how applicable they are to deterministic traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a catalog of radio types, with notes on which ones can promise messages arrive on time.

questions: which wireless technologies support deterministic networks
how does scheduling improve wireless reliability
what is the difference between wi-fi 6 and wi-fi 7
subtitle: A survey of wireless technologies suitable for reliable and available communications.

tldr.problem: Wireless networks are unreliable due to radio interference and fading, making it hard to guarantee packet delivery and low latency for critical applications like industrial control.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys four wireless technologies—Wi-Fi 6/7, TSCH, 5G, and LDACS—and their capabilities for scheduling transmissions, using frequency hopping, packet replication, and diversity techniques to achieve deterministic performance.
tldr.outcome: The document shows that modern wireless technologies have sufficient features to support Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) services when combined with proper network-layer control.

today: RFC 9913 is an Informational RFC surveying the state of wireless technology as of April 2026. It has not been obsoleted and stands as the current guidance on RAW-capable wireless technologies.

sections.title: Introduction to Reliable Wireless
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a set of techniques that let networks carry critical data flows with guaranteed delivery and bounded latency. DetNet usually works over wired networks like Ethernet, but the wireless medium is far more hostile: radio signals fade, interfere with each other, and are blocked by obstacles. This document surveys four wireless technologies that have the features DetNet needs: Wi-Fi (802.11ax and 802.11be), TSCH (a low-power time-slotted standard), 5G (3GPP NR), and LDACS (for aviation).

Making wireless reliable and available requires more than just wired DetNet. The RFC identifies lower-layer techniques that wireless systems can use: automatic repeat requests (retrying failed transmissions), frequency hopping to dodge interference, spatial diversity (sending the same data on multiple paths), and careful scheduling to reserve time and frequency resources. RAW is the DetNet architecture adapted for wireless, placing a network-layer control loop that monitors performance, computes paths, and dynamically adjusts which routes to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless is harder than wires because radio waves can bounce, interfere, or get blocked. By using smart tricks like scheduling who talks when, bouncing signals around obstacles, and sending copies on different channels, modern radio systems can promise reliable delivery.

sections.title: Scheduling and Diversity for Reliability
sections.content:
The key insight for reliable wireless is scheduling. Instead of letting all devices compete for the channel (as in traditional WiFi with CSMA), a centralized scheduler assigns each device specific times and frequencies to transmit. This eliminates collisions and allows tight control of latency. Scheduling also enables time-domain diversity: if a transmission fails, the same packet can be retried on a different frequency at a different time, helping it evade interference and fading.

Spatial diversity amplifies reliability by replicating packets and sending them over multiple paths, so that loss on one path does not mean loss of the entire packet. At the receiver, a packet elimination function discards duplicate copies, keeping only the first to arrive. Scheduling redundant transmissions across diverse paths improves resilience and allows end-to-end latency to be guaranteed as part of the overall network schedule.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sending a letter by having the post office send five copies on different routes. One route might be blocked or slow, but at least one copy will probably arrive on time. Scheduling is like telling the post office exactly when and which route each copy should take.

sections.title: Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7
sections.content:
Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax, called High Efficiency or HE) and Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be, Extreme High Throughput or EHT) introduced features that support time-sensitive applications. Both offer OFDMA—dividing the channel into subcarriers and scheduling different users across frequency and time, eliminating contention between stations. The access point (AP) can send a trigger frame to initiate multi-user uplink transmissions, giving it centralized control of medium access.

Wi-Fi 7 adds Multi-Link Operation (MLO), allowing stations to transmit and receive on multiple channels and bands simultaneously. By isolating time-sensitive traffic on dedicated bands and links, MLO reduces congestion and jitter. Both standards integrate with IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) standards, meaning a Wi-Fi network can be managed alongside Ethernet networks to provide end-to-end deterministic service. However, Wi-Fi is still subject to interference from legacy devices and the unlicensed spectrum it occupies, so RAW must combine it with other technologies for complete reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Modern Wi-Fi lets the access point tell devices exactly when they can talk, and it can assign each device its own little piece of the radio spectrum, like assigning train cars to different tracks so they do not collide.

sections.title: TSCH and 5G for Specialized Domains
sections.content:
IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH (Time-Slotted Channel Hopping) is designed for low-power industrial IoT. It splits time into slots that repeat, and each device has a schedule (called a slotframe) that specifies which channel to use at each slot. Devices synchronize tightly, avoiding collisions and enabling long sleep periods to save battery. At the IETF, the 6TiSCH working group built IPv6 support over TSCH, defining a Track as a reserved path with scheduled cells for each hop. A central Path Computation Element (PCE) computes Tracks and configures the schedule on each node.

5G (3GPP NR) is a licensed-spectrum cellular standard with centralized scheduling and native support for deterministic flows. It offers sub-millisecond latencies, high reliability (error rates below one in one hundred thousand), and redundancy through dual connectivity and multi-TRP (multiple transmission and reception points). 5G Release 16 integrated TSN, treating the 5G system as a virtual TSN bridge. Release 18 adds direct DetNet support. While TSN is the primary DetNet subnetwork, 5G can carry TSN traffic and provide the time synchronization, scheduling, and reliable delivery that RAW needs.
sections.plainLanguage: TSCH is like a train schedule: each device knows exactly when and on which track its turn is, with no surprises. 5G is a licensed cellular network where the operator controls every transmission, guaranteeing time and reliability for critical apps.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
This RFC is a survey, not a standard. It does not define protocols or practices, but documents the state of wireless technology as of publication. Each technology—Wi-Fi, TSCH, 5G, and LDACS—provides standards or specifications from its own standards body (IEEE, 3GPP, ICAO). The focus is on what features each technology offers that RAW might leverage, not on security, which is the responsibility of the underlying layer standards.

Practical RAW deployment will likely combine multiple technologies. An industrial facility might use Wi-Fi 7 indoors with 5G as a fallback, or a mesh of TSCH nodes feeding into an Ethernet backbone. The DetNet and RAW architectures provide the network-layer logic to choose paths, monitor performance, and replicate packets across diverse links.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a menu of options. Real systems will mix and match—using Wi-Fi here, 5G there, TSCH somewhere else—coordinated by a smart network layer that picks the best route and route options in real time.
